title: Trade
summary: Local, national and international trade, imports and exports, the balance of trade, South Africa's main trading products and partners, fair trade and trade barriers.

notes.text: The buying and selling (or exchange) of goods and services.

items: **Local trade**: within a community, e.g. buying vegetables at a market.
**National (internal) trade**: between different parts of a country, e.g. fruit from the Western Cape sold in Gauteng.

notes.text: Countries trade because no country can produce everything it needs efficiently. Differences in climate, natural resources, skills and technology mean that each country is better at producing certain things.
Imports, exports and the balance of trade
A good or service sold to another country.
A good or service bought from another country.

notes.latex: \text{balance of trade} = \text{value of exports} - \text{value of imports}

items: **Trade surplus** (favourable balance): exports are worth more than imports.
**Trade deficit** (unfavourable balance): imports are worth more than exports.

notes.title: Calculating the balance of trade
notes.problem: In one month a country exported goods worth R160 billion and imported goods worth R175 billion. Calculate the balance of trade and say whether it is a surplus or a deficit.

rows: Platinum group metals, gold, coal, iron ore, chrome and manganese
Citrus fruit, grapes, wine and wool

notes.text: South Africa's biggest trading partners include **China**, the **European Union** (especially Germany), the **USA**, **India**, **Japan** and other African countries, especially in the **Southern African Development Community (SADC)**. South Africa is also part of **BRICS** (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, with newer members) and the **African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)**.

notes.label: Key idea
notes.text: Many developing countries, including South Africa, export **raw materials** (primary products) and import **manufactured goods**. Manufactured goods are worth more, so countries earn more and create more jobs when they **beneficiate** (process) raw materials before exporting them.

items: **Tariffs**: taxes on imported goods that make them more expensive, protecting local industries.
**Quotas**: limits on the amount of a product that may be imported.
**Subsidies**: government payments to local producers (e.g. farmers in Europe and the USA), which make it hard for poorer countries to compete.
**Free trade agreements** remove or reduce these barriers between member countries.

notes.text: A system that guarantees small farmers and workers in developing countries a fair, stable price for products such as coffee, cocoa, tea and rooibos, plus extra money for community projects.
